companyCaseStudy.title: How Cloudflare Absorbed 1.35 Tbps and 17M RPS Attacks — anycast, edge scrubbing, and caching to keep customers up
companyCaseStudy.summary: When a single customer faced an amplified 1.35 Tbps memcached attack (and later attacks pushing 10s of millions of HTTP RPS), Cloudflare kept the site online. This story shows how distribution, edge filtering, and cache-first thinking turned catastrophic traffic into an operational non-event.
companyCaseStudy.explanation:
## Hook

Imagine a flood of traffic that, if focused on one origin, would instantly saturate every network link you own. In February 2018 a huge memcached amplification attack peaked at ~1.35 Tbps; more recently, Cloudflare has mitigated Layer 7 floods that reached tens of millions of requests per second. Instead of letting that crush customers, Cloudflare treated the Internet like a distributed pressure-relief valve.


## Problem — unprecedented volumetric and application-layer DDoS

- Attack types: memcached amplification (L3/L4, enormous bps), and massive HTTP floods (L7, millions–tens of millions of RPS).
- If traffic reached the origin: saturated links, overloaded web servers, failed TLS termination, and minutes-to-hours of downtime.
- Customers had heterogeneous origins (single VM, small cloud load balancer, or self-hosted data center) that couldn't scale to absorb attack traffic.


## Why this was hard (the challenges)

- Single-origin scaling: origin bandwidth and CPU are finite. 1.35 Tbps is far beyond most customers' capacity.
- L7 stealth: HTTP floods look like real requests, making simple blackholing risky (risk of collateral damage).
- Speed of attack ramp: attacks ramped to full intensity in seconds — manual responses are too slow.
- Global footprint: attackers used many sources; mitigation must be global to avoid local hotspots.


## Solution — engineering choices and architecture

Cloudflare's playbook that turned this from "bring down the site" to "no-op for the customer":

1. Anycast distribution: advertise customer IPs from 200+ datacenters so attack traffic is spread globally, not concentrated on a single link.
2. Edge-first filtering: do as much work at the network edge as possible (SYN cookies, rate limiting, discard malicious UDP amplification payloads, WAF at edge).
3. Cache everything and push TLS termination to edge to reduce origin load.
4. Automated rule orchestration: push firewall/rate-limit/challenge rules in seconds across the fleet.
5. Origin hardening: Argo Tunnel (cloudflared) to hide origin IPs and protect backend from direct attacks.
6. Fast-path scrubbing: specialized code paths (BPF/eBPF, high-performance packet processing) to handle millions of pps without CPU exhaustion.


### Architecture (how requests/attacks flow)

```mermaid
graph LR
  ClientAttackers[Attacking Clients]
  LegitClients[Legitimate Clients]
  ClientAttackers -->|Anycast routes| AnycastEdge
  LegitClients -->|Anycast routes| AnycastEdge
  AnycastEdge[Cloudflare Anycast Edge (200+ PoPs)] --> WAF[WAF & Rate Limiting]
  WAF --> Cache[Cache / CDN]
  Cache --> Origin[Customer Origin]
  WAF --> Scrub[Fast-path Scrubbing / SYN cookies / UDP drop]
  Scrub -->|Drop malicious| Null
  Cache -->|Cache hit -> serve| LegitClients
  Cache -->|Miss| Origin
```


## Concrete techniques and why they matter

- Anycast: spreads attack traffic to thousands of network links. Instead of one link taking 1.35 Tbps, that traffic is sharded across many PoPs — each PoP only deals with a small slice.
- Edge TLS termination + CDN caching: terminate TLS at the edge and serve cached responses directly. If 70% of requests are cacheable, the origin load drops dramatically.
- Rate limiting + JS challenges: automated edge rules raise the friction for suspicious traffic while letting legitimate users through.
- UDP amplification mitigation: drop known amplifier responses (e.g., memcached UDP) at the edge and prevent reflection by filtering out malicious UDP payloads.
- Automated playbooks: Infrastructure that lets operators create and propagate mitigation rules globally within seconds is crucial — attacks escalate quickly.


## Before / After (impact)

| Metric | Before (origin-only) | After (Cloudflare edge + scrubbing) |
|--------|----------------------:|------------------------------------:|
| Effective origin bandwidth needed to survive attack | 1.35 Tbps (impossible) | ~0 (edge absorbs) |
| Customer downtime risk during attack | High — minutes to hours | ~0 — many mitigations are transparent |
| Latency to user (under normal load) | 200–500 ms (depends on origin) | 50–120 ms (edge-terminated) |
| Cache hit ratio (example) | 30–40% | 60–80% (cache-first policies) |
| Time to deploy mitigation rules | Manual, minutes+ | Seconds (automated rules)


## Results — real numbers and outcomes

- Absorbed a 1.35 Tbps memcached amplification attack (publicly reported) without pushing traffic to the origin.
- Mitigated application-layer floods measured in the tens of millions of HTTP requests per second by shifting blocking and challenges to the edge.
- Customers experienced near-zero downtime even during the largest attacks; typical user latency fell due to edge caching.


## Operational and engineering lessons

- Design for distribution: if you can move work to many geographically distributed points, you avoid single-link saturation.
- Automate rule deployment and have pre-made playbooks for common attack patterns.
- Treat cache-first as a performance and reliability lever — caching is both faster and a DDoS absorber.
- Hide and protect origins — do not expose origin IPs to the public when using a scrubbing/CDN provider.


## Visual flowchart — quick mitigation path

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  A[Sudden spike detected] --> B{Layer?}
  B -->|L3/L4| C[Apply SYN cookies / UDP drop / Anycast sharding]
  B -->|L7| D[Edge WAF rules + Rate limit + JS challenge]
  C --> E[Scrubbed at Edge]
  D --> E
  E --> F[If still heavy -> escalate to manual playbook]
  F --> G[Deploy custom rules / engage tech ops]
```


## When this approach doesn't fully solve the problem

- If traffic is entirely legitimate (e.g., flash crowd), rate limiting can hurt real users — careful rules and progressive mitigation are needed.
- If the origin must process every request (uncacheable, stateful operations), the origin must be vertically/horizontally scaled or moved behind specialized scrubbing.


## Personality note

Think of Cloudflare as building giant floodgates in dozens of cities worldwide. The attacker pours water in many places at once — Cloudflare opens the gates everywhere so no single pipe bursts.
keyTakeaways: Anycast + edge scrubbing converts a single catastrophic link failure into many tiny, manageable loads — that’s how Cloudflare absorbed 1.35 Tbps without origin failure.
Push work to the edge: TLS termination, caching, WAF and rate-limiting massively reduce origin demand and mean attacks are often harmless to customers.
Automate mitigations and keep playbooks ready; under attack, seconds matter — global rule rollout and fast-path packet handling win.

concept.title: Cache Like a Pro: When to Use Cache‑Aside, Write‑Through, and Write‑Back
concept.summary: Caching can cut latency and reduce load — but the *how* matters. This guide explains the three common caching strategies (cache‑aside, write‑through, write‑back) with analogies, diagrams, code, and practical tradeoffs so you pick the right pattern and avoid the usual pitfalls.
concept.explanation:
## Why this matters

Imagine a busy coffee shop where orders pile up and the barista must check the recipe book for every drink. Caching is like keeping the most popular recipes on a sticky note at the counter — orders get served fast and the shop doesn't bottleneck on the recipe book. But where you put that sticky note and when you update it determine whether customers get the right drink and whether staff stay sane.

Caching strategy solves two fundamental problems:
- Reduce tail latency and database load for hot reads.
- Keep data *correct enough* for your application's correctness needs.

Pick the wrong strategy and you either suffer stale data, write amplification, complexity, or wasted memory.

---

## Analogy: Library vs. Personal Shelf

- Database = Main library (authoritative, slow to fetch).
- Cache = Your personal shelf of frequently-read books.

Cache‑aside: You check your shelf first. If it’s missing, you fetch from the library and put a copy on your shelf.
Write‑through: Every time you add a note to a book, you put it on your shelf *and* immediately send a copy to the library — both stay consistent.
Write‑back: You write on your shelf and defer updating the library until later — fast, but riskier if your shelf is lost.

---

## How each strategy works (visual)

### Cache‑Aside (lazy loading) — the most common

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
  Client->>App: Read Request(key)
  App->>Cache: GET key
  Cache-->>App: Hit / Miss
  alt Hit
    App-->>Client: Return cached value
  else Miss
    App->>DB: SELECT value FROM table WHERE key
    DB-->>App: value
    App->>Cache: SET key value
    App-->>Client: Return value
  end
```

### Write‑Through (synchronous writes)

flowchart TD
  Client[Client] --> App[App Service]
  App --> Cache[Cache]
  App --> DB[Primary DB]
  Cache -->|Read| App
  DB -->|Authoritative| App
  note right of App: Writes go to cache and DB synchronously

### Write‑Back (deferred writes)

flowchart TD
  Client --> App
  App --> Cache
  Cache -->|Background flush| DB
  note right of Cache: Writes acknowledged when saved in cache; flushed later

---

## Comparison table: quick pros/cons

| Approach | Pros | Cons | When to Use |
|----------|------|------|-------------|
| Cache‑Aside | Simple, explicit invalidation, no redundant writes | First read misses, more app logic | Most read‑heavy workloads where occasional miss is OK |
| Write‑Through | Stronger read consistency, simple concept | Higher write latency, writes doubled | When reads must see latest writes immediately and write volume is moderate |
| Write‑Back | Very low write latency, fewer DB writes (batching) | Risk of data loss, complex consistency & failure handling | High write throughput where eventual persistence ok and durability mechanisms exist |

---

## BEFORE / AFTER example (shopping cart reads)

| Scenario | Before (no cache) | After (cache‑aside) |
|---------|------------------:|-------------------:|
| Average read latency | 120 ms (DB roundtrip) | 10 ms (cache hit) |
| DB RPS | 5,000 | 800 |
| Complexity | Simple | Slightly more in app for misses and invalidation |

---

## When to use which (practical rules)

- Use **cache‑aside** when reads dominate and it's okay that the first access pays the DB cost. Good default for web sessions, product pages, computed results.
- Use **write‑through** when you must ensure readers see fresh writes immediately and you can tolerate write latency — e.g., config lookups, small write volume control plane.
- Use **write‑back** when write latency must be minimal and you can tolerate eventual persistence — e.g., analytics buffers, logging, high‑throughput telemetry. Only if you can accept complexity for durability.

---

## Code examples

### Cache‑Aside (Node.js + Redis)

```javascript
// pseudo-code
async function getUser(userId) {
  const cacheKey = `user:${userId}`
  const cached = await redis.get(cacheKey)
  if (cached) return JSON.parse(cached)

  const user = await db.query('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id=$1', [userId])
  if (user) {
    await redis.set(cacheKey, JSON.stringify(user), 'EX', 60 * 5) // 5m TTL
  }
  return user
}

// On update:
async function updateUser(userId, changes) {
  await db.update(...)
  await redis.del(`user:${userId}`) // invalidate
}
```

### Write‑Through sketch (synchronous)

```pseudo
function updateItem(id, payload):
  cache.set(key, payload)         // write to cache
  db.write(id, payload)           // write to DB (block until success)
  return ok
```

### Write‑Back sketch (deferred)

```pseudo
function updateItem(id, payload):
  cache.set(key, payload)         // write and acknowledge immediately
  scheduleFlush(key)              // background flush to DB batcher
```

---

## Common pitfalls & how to avoid them

- Stale reads: TTLs help, but design for acceptable staleness. Use versioning or cache invalidation on writes.
- Cache stampede: Many concurrent misses causing DB overload. Mitigate with request coalescing / singleflight, early recompute, or mutexes per key.
- Inconsistency (write‑through vs cache‑aside): In cache‑aside you must invalidate or update cache after DB writes — forgetting to do so causes stale results.
- Data loss with write‑back: Ensure durable staging (append log, replicated cache) and handle crashes; accept complexity.
- Evictions: Eviction policies (LRU) may remove hot items unexpectedly — monitor cache hit ratio and size.
- Hidden latency: Synchronous write‑through doubles write latency. Measure end‑to‑end.

---

## Operational considerations

- Monitor metrics: cache hit ratio, cache eviction rate, DB RPS on cache misses, TTL expiration rates.
- Start simple: implement cache‑aside first unless you have clear reasons for other strategies.
- Capacity planning: size the cache for your working set. Use sharding/replication as needed.
- Protect DB: even with caching, plan for cache failures (graceful degradation, circuit breakers, rate limiting).

---

## Quick checklist before choosing

- How fresh must reads be? (Strict -> write‑through)
- Are reads much more common than writes? (Yes -> cache‑aside)
- Can you tolerate more complexity for lower write latency? (Yes -> write‑back)
- Can you implement durability safeguards? (Required for write‑back)

---

## TL;DR

- Default to **cache‑aside** for most read‑heavy services: simple and reliable.
- Choose **write‑through** when you need readers to immediately see writes and can accept higher write latency.
- Choose **write‑back** only when write latency and write throughput are critical and you can handle durability/complexity.

Keep the coffee shop analogy in mind: caching makes everything faster, but you must decide where to keep the sticky notes, who updates them, and what happens if they blow away in the wind.
keyTakeaways: Default to cache‑aside for most read‑heavy workloads; it's simple and robust.
Write‑through gives fresher reads at the cost of write latency; write‑back gives low write latency but increases durability risk.
Plan for cache stampedes, evictions, and monitor hit rates — cache is an optimization layer, not a source of truth.
